chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Mahboub, from Ibn Raib, from Abu Al-Wardi, who said:

I said to Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) or Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), 'May Allah keep you well. An insane man attacked a man, so the insane one struck him with a strike. The man grabbed the sword from the insane man, struck him, and killed him.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'I see that he would not be killed (for it), nor would he be fined his blood money (diyah), and his blood money would be upon the Imam, and his blood would not be invalidated.'

key_terms.عَلَى الْإِمَامِ: Upon the Imam (paid from public treasury)
key_terms.يُبْطَلُ دَمُهُ: His blood is invalidated (liable for killing)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a sane man killing an insane man in self-defense according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Kafi*, the Imam establishes that a sane individual who kills an insane person in self-defense is exempt from *qisas* (retaliation) and personal *diyah* liability, with the blood money drawn from the Imam's treasury (*bayt al-mal*). This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential principle that the insane are not fully accountable for their actions, thereby protecting the defender from financial burden while preserving the validity of his life. The case highlights the distinction between intentional homicide and defensive action against those lacking full legal capacity (*ahliyyah*).
